Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in cancer cells, metabolic stress triggers specific post-translational modifications of NSUN2—such as phosphorylation or ubiquitination—which impair its methyltransferase function and lead to a targeted reduction in m5C modifications on certain tRNAs. This hypomethylation predisposes the tRNAs to cleavage by angiogenin, resulting in the generation of a distinct subset of tRNA-derived fragments. Far from being passive by-products, these tRFs actively function as molecular switches by displacing key translation initiation factors and promoting ribosome biogenesis, thus reprogramming the translational apparatus to preferentially synthesize proteins that enable cell survival and metabolic adaptation. Additionally, we propose that cross-talk with the mTORC1–c-Myc–SIRT4 signaling axis—which regulates methyl donor availability—further modulates the extent of tRNA hypomethylation and reinforces the translational shift. To test this integrated model, we will deploy contemporary technologies including mass spectrometry-based chemoproteomics to detail NSUN2 modifications, single-cell and spatial epitranscriptomics to map tRNA and tRF landscapes, and CRISPR-based interventions combined with ribosome profiling to dissect the causative role of tRFs in altering translation.
Abstract: In this study, we propose that metabolic stress in cancer cells initiates a multifaceted cascade that involves stress-induced post-translational modifications (PTMs) of the RNA methyltransferase NSUN2, thereby reducing its ability to install m5C modifications on a defined subset of tRNAs. The resulting hypomethylated tRNAs become preferential substrates for angiogenin-mediated cleavage, leading to the accumulation of specific tRNA-derived fragments (tRFs). These tRFs are not merely degradation products but function as dynamic molecular switches: they displace key translation initiation factors and concurrently promote ribosome biogenesis, selectively enhancing the translation of mRNAs encoding proteins essential for cell survival and metabolic adaptation. Importantly, this NSUN2/tRF pathway is integrated with parallel regulatory axes—such as the mTORC1–c-Myc–SIRT4 signaling cascade that modulates methyl donor (SAM) availability—to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the metabolic reprogramming observed in liver cancer and other metabolic stress contexts. To systematically interrogate this revised model, we will leverage advanced chemoproteomics to map NSUN2 PTMs, single-cell epitranscriptomic profiling combined with spatial transcriptomics to capture the spatiotemporal dynamics of tRF production, and ribosome profiling alongside CRISPR-based gene-editing to validate the functional impact of the tRF-mediated regulation of translation.
CausalChain: Metabolic stress in cancer cells -> NSUN2 post-translational modifications (phosphorylation/ubiquitination) -> Decreased NSUN2 activity and reduced m5C modification on specific tRNAs -> Enhanced susceptibility of hypomethylated tRNAs to angiogenin cleavage -> Accumulation of functionally active tRFs -> tRFs displace translation initiation factors and promote ribosome biogenesis -> Selective translation of survival and metabolic adaptation mRNAs -> Enhanced tumor cell survival under metabolic stress
